power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Rising nighttime temperatures menace sleep, yet evidence from large longitudinal studies combining objective and subjective sleep measures remains limited.
Here, we therefore examined associations of nocturnal air and wet-bulb temperature with seven sleep parameters, including possible delayed effects.
We analysed wearable-derived and subjective sleep data from 326 home-care workers (270 women) in Switzerland between June and Early October 2025, resulting in 14,290 participant-nights.
Nocturnal air temperature and humidity data were obtained from the dense MeteoSwiss monitoring network (mean distance from participants' homes, 8.6 km).

Bayesian multilevel models estimated nonlinear samenight within-person and between-person associations, while exploratory lag models examined whether associations with nocturnal temperature were also evident for exposures one and two nights earlier.
Sleep maintenance efficiency, the primary outcome, showed no meaningful association with nocturnal air temperature.
In contrast, warmer-than-usual nights were associated with shorter total sleep time and poorer subjective sleep quality.
Compared with a participant's usual exposure, total sleep time was 13.3 min shorter at +5°C, while subjective sleep-quality scores worsened by 1.2 points.
At +5°C, the probability of sleeping less than 7 h was 10.6 percentage points higher than at -4°C relative to a participant's usual exposure.
Changes in sleep-stage percentages and recovery index were very small.
Wet-bulb results were broadly comparable while exploratory lag analyses provided little evidence of consistent delayed effects.
Higher nocturnal ambient temperatures were associated with shorter and poorer sleep, with no evidence of short-term compensatory patterns.
The results thus underline that sleep disturbances may represent an important pathway linking warming nights to human health.
High nocturnal temperatures are a well-known challenge for human sleep worldwide.

When the Lancet Countdown report on health and climate change adopted "sleep hours lost due to high temperatures" as a health indicator, scientists showed that, compared to a 1986-2005 baseline, the sleep hours lost had increased by another record of 9 % in 2024 (+3 % from 2023; Romanello et al., 2025) and remained at a substantially elevated level compared to the historical baseline in 2025 (Romanello et al., 2026).

text.text: The main mechanism by which high nocturnal ambient temperatures impair sleep is by hampering thermoregulation.
Human body temperature follows a circadian rhythm (i.e., period length of ≈ 24 hours) peaking in the early evening hours and reaching its nadir in the early morning (Kräuchi, 2002).

text.text: To achieve these temperature variations, the body balances heat production with heat loss, where the skin at hands and feet are particularly important (Aschoff, 1956; Kräuchi & Wirz-Justice, 2001).

text.text: Laboratory studies usually investigating the effects of heat on sleep in young volunteers using gold-standard sleep assessment with polysomnography (PSG) consistently found that heat increased nocturnal wakefulness thereby reducing sleep efficiency, that is the percentage of time in bed spent asleep (Ioannou et al., 2024; Libert et al., 1988; Okamoto-Mizuno et al., 2005; Tsuzuki et al., 2004).

text.text: Furthermore, high ambient temperatures decreased rapid eye-movement (REM) sleep (Libert et al., 1988) and deep non-REM sleep proportions (Bonegio et al., 1988; Lan et al., 2014; Okamoto-Mizuno et al., 2005; Tsuzuki et al., 2004), increased sleep fragmentation (Libert et al., 1988), and delayed sleep onset latency (Lan et al., 2014).

text.text: Naturalistic studies have assessed the effects of seasonal temperature variations on sleep using mostly actimetry, that is an assessment of rest-activity patterns to estimate for instance sleep duration.

More recently, consumer sleeptracking devices have enabled the longitudinal assessment of objective sleep markers beyond just the duration of the resting phase in larger samples (Mattingly et al., 2021).

text.text: In community-dwelling older adults followed across one year, increasing bedroom temperature from 20-25°C to 25-30°C was associated with meaningful reductions in sleep efficiency (i.e., the percentage of sleep among time spent in bed), sleep duration, and restfulness (Baniassadi et al., 2023).

text.text: In a large international study using wearable-derived sleep data from more than 47,000 participants across 68 countries, Minor et al. (2022) found that higher minimal temperatures shortened sleep, primarily by delaying sleep onset.

text.text: This effect was stronger in women and older adults, and the authors concluded there was no evidence of adaptation to warmer temperatures.

However, exposure assessment was somewhat limited, the nearest weather station could be up to 100 km from an individual's location, weather data were available only at daily resolution level, and subjective sleep information was not available.
Thus, there is a need for longitudinal studies combining objective and subjective sleep assessments with high-resolution environmental exposure data.

Moreover, delayed effects of heat exposure on sleep, including possible compensatory responses across subsequent nights remain poorly characterised, although lagged effects have repeatedly been documented for other health outcomes such as mortality or hospital admissions (Bobb et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2025).

text.text: Therefore, we here sought to investigate concurrent and delayed associations between nocturnal heat exposure and objective and subjective sleep in healthcare workers providing home care in Switzerland.

Additionally, we explored whether higher ambient temperatures, that is, air and wet-bulb temperature, affected mental wellbeing (Thompson et al., 2018; Thompson et al., 2023), for which sleep likely is a mediator (Freeman et al., 2020), and whether an app providing tips on coping with heat could reduce heat-related sleep disturbances (Gerosa et al., 2025).

text.text: To this end, we used a three-month longitudinal dataset collected from 342 home-care workers in Switzerland during the summer of 2025, including subjective and wearable-derived sleep measures alongside other assessments.

The physically demanding nature of home care work and frequent travel between clients' homes, in combination with increased workload during heat events, render this occupational group particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of high temperatures (Fortunato et al., 2026).

text.text: We hypothesised that Sleep Maintenance Efficiency (SME), our primary outcome, would decrease with increasing nocturnal temperature.

Note that because the wearable device did not detect wakefulness before sleep onset or after final awakening, this measure reflects wakefulness during the sleep period rather than total sleep efficiency.
Secondary (exploratory) outcomes were device-derived total sleep time, recovery index, percentages of light, deep, and REM sleep, and daily subjective sleep quality assessed with a sleep diary.
We expected total sleep time, nocturnal recovery, deep, and REM sleep proportions as well as subjective sleep quality to decrease and light sleep proportions to increase with increasing temperatures.

In exploratory analyses, we additionally examined whether temperatures were associated with sleep variables not only during the concurrent night, but also with temperatures on the preceding one and two nights.

Beyond this, we hypothesised that higher ambient temperatures would negatively impact participants' mental wellbeing and that the app-based intervention would ameliorate the effects of ambient temperature on sleep compared to the control group.

The full sample comprised 342 home-care workers from the German-and Italian-speaking parts of Switzerland, who were recruited to participate in the REHEAT study between June and Early October 2025 (for the published protocol, see Gerosa et al., 2025).

The majority of participants (n = 218; 67 %) worked in the canton of Ticino (i.e., southern Switzerland), and 108 participants (33 %) in northeastern Switzerland.
Many were nurses (n = 185; 56.7 %), 71 (21.8 %) described themselves as care workers, 50 (15.3 %) had the role of a nursing assistant and 20 (6.1 %) indicated they had a different profession.

For the duration of the study, the participants received daily prompts to complete a diary to assess various symptoms.
Here, they indicated whether they had worked the previous day, if yes, in which shift they worked (4-hour time slots from 7 am the previous day until 7 am that day).
If they had not worked, they were asked to provide a reason (i.e., "Weekend, public holiday, or vacation", "Illness", "Injury", "Other reason").
They also had to indicate whether they had slept at home and if they had worked the night.
Note that we excluded days on which participants had worked a night shift (i.e., between 10 pm and 7 am) as well as the following night.

For the duration of the study, participants continuously wore a Garmin Vivosmart 5 or Garmin Venu Sq 2 wearable device, from which we derived objective sleep metrics.
They were instructed to wear the device as much as possible except for e.g., charging, sauna, or longer hot baths.
Specifically, we looked at Sleep Maintenance Efficiency, which refers to the ratio between sleep duration and the time between the onset of sleep and the final awakening (primary endpoint).
Note that Sleep Efficiency referring to the ratio between actual sleep duration and the time between lights off and getting up, which has been used in prior studies, is not provided by Garmin.

Secondary outcomes included the percentage of light sleep (i.e., N1 and N2 according to scoring criteria of the American Association of Sleep Medicine [AASM]; Troester et al., 2023), percentage of deep sleep, and percentage of Rapid-Eye Movement (REM) sleep as well as a recovery index, which is the ratio between the actual increase (or decrease in some cases) in "body battery" overnight relative to the available increase.

text.text: Each participant was assigned to the geographically nearest eligible MeteoSwiss station, which had to provide hourly observations and be at an altitude of ≤1000 m a.s.l. to avoid assigning high-altitude stations unlikely to represent residential exposure conditions.
In total, we identified 15 relevant stations and the mean distance between home addresses and the nearest MeteoSwiss station was 8.6 ± 5.1 km (range 0.7 -23.8 km).
Hourly meteorological data were obtained from MeteoSwiss Open Data for the MeteoSwiss weather station assigned to each participants' home location.
Data were retrieved via the MeteoSwiss STAC API (ch.meteoschweiz.ogd-smn) for the study period from 6 June 2025 (first participant in) to 6 October 2025 (last participant out).
From the hourly station files, air temperature at 2 m above ground (tre200h0) and relative humidity at 2 m above ground (ure200h0) were extracted.
Nocturnal exposure windows were defined in local time from 23:00 to 07:00.
Each sleep-window date therefore comprised nine hourly observations: 23:00 on the evening of the sleep-window date and 00:00-07:00 on the following day or morning.
For each station and sleep-window date, nocturnal mean air temperature was subsequently calculated from the hourly observations.

In addition, hourly wet-bulb temperature was estimated from air temperature and relative humidity using the Stull approximation (Stull, 2011), and the nocturnal mean wet-bulb temperature was as the average across the sleep window.

Daily heat indicators were derived from station-level hourly data aggregated by local calendar day.

The 24-h daily mean temperature (Tmean) identified warm-day sequences, while daily maximum temperature identified hot days (≥30°C), heat waves (≥3 consecutive days with Tmean ≥25°C), and hot spells (1-2 consecutive days with Tmean ≥25°C).
Participants were excluded if participants reported pregnancy at baseline or offboarding (n = 6) or if the assigned MeteoSwiss station was more than 25 km from the home address (n = 8).
Participant-nights were excluded if someone did not sleep at home or did not answer this question on a specific day (n = 11719).
Additionally, nights for which participants reported evening or night work between 19:00 and 07:00 were excluded (n = 2264).
We additionally excluded the nights following evening or night work (n = 1104) and finally excluded nights following a day on which participants reported illness (n = 267).
This resulted in retention of 14290 nights (46.1 %) from 326 participants.
Finally, Garmin recovery index data were only deemed valid after 7 nights of collected data.

text.text: Climate change poses growing risks to human health, and for sleep, nighttime temperatures are particularly relevant.
As nights warm rapidly, rising temperatures may increasingly threaten sleep, an important determinant of health (Minor et al., 2026).
text.formatted: As nights warm rapidly, rising temperatures may increasingly threaten sleep, an important determinant of health <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Minor et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Leveraging ambient meteorological data from the dense MeteoSwiss monitoring network, objective sleep data and subjective sleep ratings from up to 14,290 participant-nights, this study extends evidence that warmer nights are associated with shorter sleep duration, a higher probability of short sleep, and poorer subjective sleep quality.
Cooler nights showed the opposite pattern, while exploratory analyses provided little evidence of short-term compensatory patterns.

More specifically, in our sample of home-care workers in northeastern and southern Switzerland, total sleep time was approximately 6 minutes shorter when nocturnal air temperature was 3°C higher than a participant's usual exposure and about 13 minutes shorter at +5°C. We consider these differences meaningful, particularly as previous research suggests limited compensation for heat-related sleep loss on subsequent nights (Libert et al., 1988; Minor et al., 2022).
text.formatted: More specifically, in our sample of home-care workers in northeastern and southern Switzerland, total sleep time was approximately 6 minutes shorter when nocturnal air temperature was 3°C higher than a participant's usual exposure and about 13 minutes shorter at +5°C. We consider these differences meaningful, particularly as previous research suggests limited compensation for heat-related sleep loss on subsequent nights <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Libert et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Minor et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, subjective sleep quality worsened by 0.6 scale points (range 4-20) at +3°C and by 1.2 scale points at +5°C with the deterioration slightly more pronounced in older individuals.
This is consistent with previous findings suggesting that heat has a greater impact on sleep in older adults (Li et al., 2025; Minor et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This is consistent with previous findings suggesting that heat has a greater impact on sleep in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Li et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Minor et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, we found little indication that the intervention was able to attenuate these temperature-related changes.

This suggests that practical tips (e.g., to take a lukewarm shower before going to bed, to ventilate the room when it is cool outside) alone may have limited potential to reduce the physiological sensitivity of sleep to high ambient temperatures.

Exploratory analyses based on absolute nocturnal air temperature supported this pattern: Compared with 17°C, lower temperatures were associated with longer sleep duration and better subjective sleep quality, whereas higher temperatures were associated with shorter sleep duration and worse subjective sleep quality.
Across the modelled range, predicted total sleep time decreased by almost 24 minutes from 11°C to 24°C, while subjective sleep quality worsened by approximately 1.8 scale points.
Note that these temperatures refer to outdoor air temperatures with nocturnal indoor temperatures likely being even higher, especially during the warm season.
Results for nocturnal wet-bulb temperature, which additionally accounts for relative humidity besides air temperature, were broadly comparable in magnitude.

The practical relevance of these results is underscored by the progressively increasing probability of short sleep at higher air temperatures, whether expressed as absolute air temperature or as warmer-than-usual nights.

For example, the estimated probability of sleeping less than 7 h, a commonly used threshold for short sleep (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015), increased from about 53 % at 11°C to 68 % at 24°C, a difference of almost 15 percentage points.

text.text: For the more stringent <6 h threshold, warmer nights were likewise associated with a higher probability of short sleep.
text.formatted: For the more stringent <6 h threshold, warmer nights were likewise associated with a higher probability of short sleep.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that even relatively modest temperature-related reductions in average sleep duration may translate into a meaningful increase in the frequency of nights falling below established sleep-duration thresholds.

Additionally, previous research provided little evidence for short-term compensatory responses or for medium-to long-term adaptation over months or years, suggesting that even moderate reductions in total sleep time may accumulate across repeated warm nights (Libert et al., 1988; Minor et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Additionally, previous research provided little evidence for short-term compensatory responses or for medium-to long-term adaptation over months or years, suggesting that even moderate reductions in total sleep time may accumulate across repeated warm nights <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Libert et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Minor et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Our exploratory lag analyses supported this interpretation.
They assessed whether temperature on preceding nights was associated with sleep on the outcome night after accounting for temperature on that same night.
We found little evidence of consistent delayed or compensatory patterns.

Higher temperature on the outcome night was associated with shorter total sleep time and worse subjective sleep quality, whereas associations with temperatures on preceding nights were weaker and inconsistent.
Some alternating patterns were observed for sleep-stage percentages and the recovery index, but these differences were negligible in magnitude.
Overall, the findings provided little evidence of a systematic rebound following warmer nights.
However, because the lag analyses examined prior-night temperature rather than prior-night sleep loss, they cannot directly determine whether sleep loss was compensated for on subsequent nights.
The temperature-related reduction in sleep duration observed in our study was larger than that reported by Minor et al. (2022).
text.formatted: The temperature-related reduction in sleep duration observed in our study was larger than that reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Minor et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Linking more than 7 million wearablederived sleep records from 68 countries to minimum nighttime temperature, they observed a considerably shallower decline in sleep duration, with their published response curve suggesting a reduction of approximately 5 minutes between 11°C and 24°C. Direct quantitative comparison is limited, however, because the studies used different temperature metrics, with mean nocturnal temperature in the present study and minimum daily temperature in Minor and colleagues' study.

Additionally, home care workers' sleep may be particularly susceptible to heat, as workload often increases during heat episodes, adding psychological stress to the physical strain of their work (Fortunato et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Additionally, home care workers' sleep may be particularly susceptible to heat, as workload often increases during heat episodes, adding psychological stress to the physical strain of their work <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fortunato et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In a longitudinal dataset of adults aged over 65 years, the response curve reported by Baniassadi et al. (2023) suggests a decline of roughly 30 minutes in total sleep time between approximately 15°C and 25°C, which is more in line with our estimates.

(2023)</ref> suggests a decline of roughly 30 minutes in total sleep time between approximately 15°C and 25°C, which is more in line with our estimates.

text.text: However, unlike the present study, the researchers measured indoor temperature directly in participants' bedrooms, which limits direct comparison of effect sizes in addition to the participants' age.

Unlike previous laboratory studies (Ioannou et al., 2024; Libert et al., 1988; Okamoto-Mizuno et al., 2005; Tsuzuki et al., 2004), we found no meaningful changes in sleep maintenance efficiency (SME) or sleep stage proportions with varying ambient temperatures, although temperature-related decreases in REM sleep were more pronounced in older individuals underlining their increased sensitivity to increasing nocturnal temperatures.
text.formatted: Unlike previous laboratory studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Ioannou et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Libert et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Okamoto-Mizuno et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Tsuzuki et al., 2004)</ref>, we found no meaningful changes in sleep maintenance efficiency (SME) or sleep stage proportions with varying ambient temperatures, although temperature-related decreases in REM sleep were more pronounced in older individuals underlining their increased sensitivity to increasing nocturnal temperatures.

text.text: The absence of clearer effects on sleep macrostructure may partly reflect the limited accuracy of consumer sleep-tracking devices, particularly for sleep-stage classification.
An important difference is that previous studies assessed sleep efficiency, defined as total sleep time relative to the entire time spent in bed.

In contrast, the wearable-derived SME used here only captures the proportion of sleep between the first and last detected sleep episodes and therefore excludes time spent awake before sleep onset or after final awakening.
Additionally, while wearable devices are relatively good at detecting total sleep time, their ability to detect wakefulness after sleep onset is known to be limited (Chinoy et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Additionally, while wearable devices are relatively good at detecting total sleep time, their ability to detect wakefulness after sleep onset is known to be limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chinoy et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This could have resulted in an overestimation of SME and decreased sensitivity to changes in this metric.

Further, consumer devices' biases may have distorted night-to-night differences resulting, which could explain the absence of meaningful variations in sleep stage proportions with ambient temperature.
Specifically, validation studies show that they often systematically overestimate wake after sleep onset (WASO) and light sleep on nights with little wakefulness and objectively better sleep.
Conversely, they underestimate WASO and light sleep on 'worse' nights with more wakefulness (Chinoy et al., 2020; Kainec et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Conversely, they underestimate WASO and light sleep on 'worse' nights with more wakefulness <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chinoy et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kainec et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This bias pattern can result in a regression towards the device's mean estimate, and consequently an underestimation of inter-night variability.

The strengths of this study include the large number of participant-nights and the combination of wearable-derived objective sleep measures with subjective sleep ratings, providing complementary information on sleep under real-world conditions.

The longitudinal within-person design allowed us to examine how sleep changed when individuals experienced warmer or cooler nights than usual, thereby reducing the influence of stable between-person differences.
It also allowed us to explore possible delayed associations with temperature.

Exposure assessment was based on hourly data from the dense MeteoSwiss monitoring network and included both air temperature and humidity, enabling us to additionally examine nocturnal wet-bulb temperature in addition to air temperature.
The main limitations concern exposure and sleep measurement.
Weather-station data can only approximate the thermal conditions experienced in participants' bedrooms.
Particularly during warm periods, nighttime indoor temperatures likely remain higher than outdoor temperatures because of heat stored in buildings (Wright et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Particularly during warm periods, nighttime indoor temperatures likely remain higher than outdoor temperatures because of heat stored in buildings <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Wright et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should therefore directly record bedroom temperature and humidity, for example using iButtons (Maxim Integrated).

Objective sleep outcomes were derived from consumer wearables, which are less accurate than polysomnography, particularly for sleep staging and the detection of wakefulness (Chinoy et al., 2020; Kainec et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Objective sleep outcomes were derived from consumer wearables, which are less accurate than polysomnography, particularly for sleep staging and the detection of wakefulness <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chinoy et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kainec et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This may have limited our ability to detect small temperature-related changes in these outcomes.

At the same time, we argue that consumer wearables provide a feasible and cost-efficient approach for obtaining repeated objective sleep measurements over thousands of nights under real-world conditions.

To conclude, in a large longitudinal study of home-care workers across northeastern and southern Switzerland, higher nocturnal ambient temperatures were associated with shorter total sleep time, a greater probability of short sleep, and poorer subjective sleep quality, with no clear evidence of temporal patterns consistent with short-term compensation.
Besides direct physiological effects of heat, this could also reflect increased workload and stress due to high temperatures.

Given the widespread exposure to rising nighttime temperatures worldwide and the importance of sufficient, good-quality sleep for health, these findings point to sleep as a potentially important and underrecognized pathway through which exposure to high ambient temperature may affect human health.

Whether heat-related sleep impairment contributes to the broader adverse health effects of high temperatures, including excess mortality, hospital admissions, and poorer mental health, remains largely unknown and warrants further investigation.
